title: Q&A: Does the world need ‘carbon capture and storage’ to reach net-zero? - Carbon Brief
gist: Carbon capture and storage remains a ~62.5MtCO2/year niche business dominated by gas processing and enhanced oil recovery, yet IEA net-zero scenarios assume 1.7GtCO2 captured by 2035 — a ~30x scale-up. The demand-side story is quietly rotating away from power generation (IEA cut its power-CCS outlook by a third since 2021) and toward cement, steel, chemicals and blue hydrogen, while real-world capture rates near 50% versus a 90-95% design standard undercut the investment case.

themes.theme: CCS today is an oil-and-gas by-product, not a climate business

insights.claim: Around three-quarters of all captured CO2 worldwide is used for enhanced oil recovery — injecting CO2 into depleted wells to extract more oil — making oil production, not climate mitigation, the dominant commercial end-market for carbon capture.
insights.speaker: Josh Gabbatiss
insights.so_what: Revenue for existing capture assets is levered to crude economics, not carbon policy; a CCS 'pure play' priced on climate demand is mispricing its actual customer base.
insights.quote: This remains, by far, the most significant end use for captured CO2 worldwide, with around three-quarters of it used for this purpose.
insights.locator: What is CCS? — 'Carbon capture technology was originally rolled out'

insights.claim: Most CO2 captured today is a by-product of gas purification, where separating CO2 from methane is a required processing step and selling the CO2 improves gas project economics — meaning the cheapest existing capture volumes exist because of fossil-fuel production, not despite it.
insights.speaker: Josh Gabbatiss
insights.so_what: Cost curves quoted from legacy projects understate the cost of capture in sectors like cement where CO2 separation is not already part of the process.
insights.quote: Moreover, most of the CO2 currently captured is a by-product of gas purification
insights.locator: What is CCS? — 'Moreover, most of the CO2 currently captured'

insights.claim: Carbon capture is not a new technology risk: it was first deployed at US and Canadian oil wells in the early 1970s and first proposed as a climate measure in a 1976 academic article, so five decades of operating history have still not produced scale.
insights.speaker: Josh Gabbatiss
insights.so_what: Treat 'early-stage technology' framing sceptically — the constraint is economics and policy, not physics, so learning-curve arguments used for solar do not transfer.
insights.locator: What is CCS? — 'Carbon capture technology was originally rolled out at US and Canadian oil wells'

insights.claim: The 'CCUS' label bundles carbon utilisation — turning CO2 into fertilisers, fuels or building materials — with permanent storage, even though utilisation often releases the CO2 back to the atmosphere and delivers no permanent emissions cut.
insights.speaker: Josh Gabbatiss
insights.so_what: Screen company disclosures for 'CCUS capacity' claims that are really utilisation volumes — they will not survive tightening permanence rules in carbon accounting.
insights.quote: Such uses do not necessarily lead to permanent emissions cuts, as the CO2 can end up later being released back into the atmosphere.
insights.locator: What is CCS? — 'The term "CCUS" is sometimes also used'

themes.theme: The 30x gap between installed base and net-zero scenarios

insights.claim: As of February 2026 there were 75 operational carbon capture and storage projects worldwide capturing 62.5m tonnes of CO2 a year — roughly the annual greenhouse gas emissions of Ecuador, and a trivial fraction of emissions from global fossil-fuel use.
insights.speaker: Josh Gabbatiss
insights.so_what: The installed base is the baseline for any addressable-market model; 62.5MtCO2/year is the number to check any CCS equipment or storage TAM claim against.
insights.quote: Together, these projects capture 62.5m tonnes of CO2 (MtCO2) each year. This is equivalent to the annual greenhouse gas emissions of Ecuador.
insights.locator: How much CCS capacity has been built so far?

insights.claim: Global carbon capture capacity has grown from 22 projects capturing 40MtCO2 annually operational or under construction in 2014 to 62.5MtCO2 actually operating in 2026 — roughly 50% growth over twelve years, versus the exponential ramps assumed in climate models.
insights.speaker: Josh Gabbatiss
insights.so_what: Historical build rate is the best prior for forecasting; any model implying decades of 30%+ CAGR from here is fighting a twelve-year track record of near-stagnation.
insights.locator: How much CCS capacity has been built so far? — '(This compares with the 22 CCS projects'

insights.claim: The IEA's net-zero scenario assumes 1.7GtCO2 captured by 2035 — nearly 30 times today's volume — and the IEA has stated that reaching net-zero would be 'virtually impossible' without carbon capture and storage.
insights.speaker: Josh Gabbatiss
insights.so_what: This is the demand assumption embedded in most CCS equity narratives; the credibility of a 30x-in-nine-years ramp is the single biggest swing factor for the sector.
insights.quote: The IEA includes 1.7GtCO2 being captured by 2035 in its net-zero scenario – nearly 30 times more than is captured today.
insights.locator: What role is CCS expected to play in reaching net-zero?

insights.claim: The forward pipeline is 93.7MtCO2 of capacity under construction as of February 2026 versus 1,279.6MtCO2 merely in 'planning' — a ratio of roughly 14:1 planned-to-committed in an industry with a long history of cancellations and delays.
insights.speaker: Josh Gabbatiss
insights.so_what: Only the ~94MtCO2 with a final investment decision represents near-term orders; discount headline pipeline numbers built on concept and feasibility studies heavily.
insights.quote: 93.7MtCO2 of capture or storage capacity is under construction as of February 2026 and another 1,279.6MtCO2 is in the “planning” stages.
insights.locator: How much CCS capacity has been built so far? — 'A surge of projects have entered the global CCS pipeline'

insights.claim: Even the IEA has characterised carbon capture's history as one of unmet expectations, noting that its mitigation potential has been recognised for decades while deployment has stayed slow — an unusually blunt self-assessment from a body whose own scenarios depend on the technology.
insights.speaker: Josh Gabbatiss
insights.so_what: The main scenario-setter concedes the base rate of disappointment, which weakens the authority usually cited to justify CCS capital allocation.
insights.quote: story of CCUS has largely been one of unmet expectations: its potential to mitigate climate change has been recognised for decades, but deployment has been slow
insights.locator: How much CCS capacity has been built so far? — 'In a 2020 report, the IEA explained'

insights.claim: Carbon capture capacity is concentrated in fossil-fuel producing economies — the US and Canada dominate, with Norway, Brazil and the Gulf states as the other major contributors — so the geography of CCS tracks hydrocarbon endowment rather than emissions or climate ambition.
insights.speaker: Josh Gabbatiss
insights.so_what: Policy and subsidy risk for CCS is concentrated in petro-states; a shift in US or Canadian fiscal support moves most of the world's installed capacity economics at once.
insights.locator: How much CCS capacity has been built so far? — 'As the map below shows'

themes.theme: Power-sector CCS is being written down; industry is the residual

insights.claim: The IEA has cut its outlook for carbon capture in the power sector by a third relative to its 2021 expectations, driven by slow deployment and rapid renewables cost declines that make abated gas and coal plants less attractive.
insights.speaker: Josh Gabbatiss
insights.so_what: Vendors levered to post-combustion capture on power plants face a structurally shrinking forecast even inside official net-zero scenarios — a bearish revision that predates any policy retreat.
insights.quote: Carbon Brief analysis shows that the IEA has reduced its outlook for CCS in the power sector by a third, compared to its expectations in 2021
insights.locator: What role is CCS expected to play in reaching net-zero? — 'Carbon Brief analysis shows'

insights.claim: Under the IEA's net-zero scenario, industrial sectors — cement, steel and chemicals — account for 60% of CO2 captured in 2050, with the remaining 40% roughly split between electricity generation and blue hydrogen production.
insights.speaker: Josh Gabbatiss
insights.so_what: The long-run demand mix favours industrial capture technology and CO2 transport/storage infrastructure over power-plant retrofits — position accordingly.
insights.locator: What role is CCS expected to play in reaching net-zero? — 'Industrial sectors – particularly cement, steel and chemicals'

insights.claim: Heavy industry represents less than 10% of announced carbon capture capacity, directly contradicting the sector prioritisation that both the IEA scenarios and NGO analysis say delivers the most climate value.
insights.speaker: Josh Gabbatiss
insights.so_what: A structural mismatch between where capital is going and where policy value sits implies future project cancellations or a forced re-steering of subsidies toward cement and lime.
insights.quote: Despite this, the focus of the CCS sector so far has not been in heavy industry, which represents less than 10% of announced capacity.
insights.locator: What role is CCS expected to play in reaching net-zero? — 'Despite this, the focus of the CCS sector'

insights.claim: Bellona and E3G's 'CCS ladder' ranks cement and lime production at the top for climate value while assigning power-sector carbon capture 'low and decreasing value', giving policymakers an explicit prioritisation framework under constrained public funding.
insights.speaker: Josh Gabbatiss
insights.so_what: A ready-made rationing rubric for governments cutting CCS budgets — projects low on the ladder are the first candidates for defunding.
insights.quote: Their “CCS ladder” places CCS in cement and lime production at the top – with the highest “climate value” – while power CCS has “low and decreasing value”.
insights.locator: What role is CCS expected to play in reaching net-zero? — 'Climate NGOs Bellona and E3G have stressed'

insights.claim: Cement is the durable core of the carbon capture case because roughly 7% of global CO2 comes from cement and much of it originates in the chemical process itself, so the emissions persist even if the industry is fully electrified — the IEA calls CCS 'virtually the only technology' able to cut them significantly.
insights.speaker: Josh Gabbatiss
insights.so_what: Cement CCS demand is insulated from renewables cost deflation in a way power CCS is not — the most defensible niche if the sector consolidates.
insights.quote: The IEA describes CCS as “virtually the only technology” that can significantly cut cement emissions, which account for around 7% of the global total.
insights.locator: What role is CCS expected to play in reaching net-zero? — 'The IEA describes CCS as'

insights.claim: The category of 'hard-to-abate' emissions is shrinking as alternatives get cheaper and more available, making carbon capture less attractive in some sectors and less vital in others — the definitional boundary of the CCS market is itself moving against it.
insights.speaker: Josh Gabbatiss
insights.so_what: CCS addressable market erodes from both ends as electrification and alternative processes advance — expect further downward revisions rather than a stable floor.
insights.quote: Yet, the understanding of “hard-to-abate” emissions is changing, as alternatives to CCS become cheaper and increasingly available.
insights.locator: What role is CCS expected to play in reaching net-zero? — 'Yet, the understanding of "hard-to-abate" emissions is changing'

insights.claim: Coal power with carbon capture has effectively failed as a commercial category: only seven such plants operate worldwide — five in China, one in the US and one in Canada — after 2000s-era interest collapsed under plummeting renewable costs.
insights.speaker: Josh Gabbatiss
insights.so_what: A completed case study of how renewables deflation kills a CCS end-market; the same mechanism is now working on gas-CCS.
insights.quote: Today, there are only seven operating CCS-coal plants worldwide – five in China, one in the US and one in Canada.
insights.locator: How much CCS capacity has been built so far? — 'This interest largely petered out'

insights.claim: The UN climate-talks commitment to 'phase down' only 'unabated' coal power creates a policy loophole that could let China keep running its sizable coal fleet by fitting carbon capture, converting a phase-out pledge into a retrofit market.
insights.speaker: Josh Gabbatiss
insights.so_what: Watch Chinese coal-CCS retrofit policy as the one plausible source of very large-volume power-sector capture demand despite the IEA's downgrade.
insights.locator: What role is CCS expected to play in reaching net-zero? — 'Nations have agreed at UN climate talks'

themes.theme: Performance risk: capture rates, leakage and lifecycle emissions

insights.claim: The widespread design standard is that carbon capture projects should capture at least 90% of emitted CO2 — with UK guidelines targeting 95% — but IEEFA's 2023 analysis of operating projects concluded most fall far below those rates and continue emitting significant CO2.
insights.speaker: Josh Gabbatiss
insights.so_what: Contracted capture rates versus realised rates is the key diligence item on any CCS offtake or carbon-credit contract; the gap is where the value leaks.
insights.quote: There is a widespread view that CCS projects should aim to capture at least 90% of the CO2 being emitted. UK guidelines are among those targeting a higher capture rate of 95%.
insights.locator: Why is CCS controversial? — 'There is a widespread view that CCS projects'

insights.claim: Climate Analytics calculated in 2023 that if a high-CCS IPCC pathway were built out at the ~50% capture rates seen in existing facilities with high upstream emissions, it would add an extra 86GtCO2e by 2050 — and even the IEA's more limited net-zero scenario could add 16GtCO2e from underperforming fossil CCS.
insights.speaker: Josh Gabbatiss
insights.so_what: Quantifies the downside case where CCS deployment is net-negative for climate outcomes — a live tail risk for policy reversal and stranded CCS assets.
insights.quote: if CO2 was captured at rates seen in existing facilities – around 50% – and upstream emissions remain high, CCS use could see an extra 86GtCO2e emitted by 2050
insights.locator: Why is CCS controversial? — 'Considering these factors, in 2023 Climate Analytics assessed'

insights.claim: Capture is the most expensive stage of the carbon capture and storage chain, which creates a direct economic incentive for operators to run below the 90-95% capture rates their projects are nominally designed for.
insights.speaker: Josh Gabbatiss
insights.so_what: Explains why underperformance is systematic rather than accidental — regulation must tie subsidy to realised tonnes captured, not installed capacity.
insights.quote: (Capture is the most expensive part of the CCS process.)
insights.locator: Why is CCS controversial? — 'The thinktank concluded that, in reality'

insights.claim: Geological storage volume is not the binding constraint — the IPCC says there is ample global storage and that appropriately selected and managed sites can permanently isolate CO2 — but even low leakage rates across the transport and storage chain could have large climate impact at scale.
insights.speaker: Josh Gabbatiss
insights.so_what: Reframes the risk: storage capacity is abundant, so the bottlenecks and liabilities sit in capture economics and pipeline/monitoring integrity.
insights.locator: Why is CCS controversial? — 'Once the CO2 is captured, it must be stored'

insights.claim: A 2023 University of Oxford working paper found a low-CCS pathway to net-zero would cost around $1tn a year less than a high-CCS pathway and found no evidence of technological learning or associated cost reductions in CCS to date — while still judging CCS likely necessary for cement and chemicals.
insights.speaker: Josh Gabbatiss
insights.so_what: The absence of a learning curve is the killer finding — it means CCS cost does not fall with deployment the way solar and batteries did, undermining scale-based investment theses.
insights.quote: The researchers stated that “no evidence is found for technological learning or associated cost reductions” in the development of CCS to date.
insights.locator: Why is CCS controversial? — 'A University of Oxford working paper published in 2023'

themes.theme: The fossil-industry entanglement and its counter-argument

insights.claim: Carbon capture's dependence on the fossil-fuel industry cuts both ways: oil and gas companies have a demonstrated track record in multi-million and billion-dollar subsurface engineering projects, which is precisely the capability needed to scale CO2 storage.
insights.speaker: Josh Gabbatiss
insights.so_what: Storage execution capability is concentrated in incumbent E&P operators — the credible CO2 storage licensees are oil majors, not startups.
insights.quote: Oil and gas companies can evidence a track record in multi-million or billion-dollar subsurface engineering projects
insights.locator: Why is CCS controversial? — 'Roberts also notes that fossil-fuel companies have the experience'

insights.claim: A 2021 study co-authored by Stuart Haszeldine found that fossil-fuel companies have actually invested relatively small amounts in carbon capture compared with renewables and nature-based solutions, despite their apparent public support for the technology.
insights.speaker: Josh Gabbatiss
insights.so_what: Rhetorical support has not converted into balance-sheet commitment — a signal that majors themselves do not underwrite CCS returns without public money.
insights.locator: Why is CCS controversial? — 'Despite the fossil-fuel industry's apparent support for CCS'

insights.claim: Lund University ecological economist Lina Lefstad argues the slow pace of deployment is itself evidence against the theory that the fossil-fuel industry profits from CCS — if the industry really stood to win, large-scale CCS would already exist.
insights.speaker: Josh Gabbatiss
insights.so_what: Undercuts the dominant critique while implying something worse for investors: nobody, including the incumbents, can make CCS pay at scale.
insights.quote: People seem really worried that the fossil-fuel industry is going to come out the winner again, but if that was the case I think we would have large-scale CCS by now.
insights.locator: Why is CCS controversial? — 'Lina Lefstad at Lund University questions'

insights.claim: IEEFA energy finance analyst Andrew Reid frames the allocation question as whether decarbonising fossil fuels is worth the technical, timing and cost risk at all, concluding that if investment is to be made anywhere in CCS it most likely should be cement and chemicals.
insights.speaker: Josh Gabbatiss
insights.so_what: Even the sector's most prominent financial critic concedes an industrial CCS niche — the trade is long cement/chemicals capture, short gas-power capture.
insights.quote: As for cement and chemicals, again, there are alternatives, but these are nascent and expensive. CCS may be a solution here and if investment is going to be made in any area, it most likely should be these.
insights.locator: Why is CCS controversial? — 'All of this calls into question many uses of CCS'

insights.claim: Climate models are the mechanism that put carbon capture back on the policy agenda, since a majority of IPCC-assessed 1.5C pathways rely on CCS at fossil-fuel plants and industrial sites — meaning demand for the technology is generated by modelling assumptions before it is generated by markets.
insights.speaker: Josh Gabbatiss
insights.so_what: Model revisions are a leading indicator for CCS policy support — track IPCC and IEA scenario updates as the sector's real order book.
insights.quote: These models have been quite instrumental in bringing CCS back onto the agenda
insights.locator: What role is CCS expected to play in reaching net-zero? — 'Many global pathways that have been set out'

insights.claim: Reaching net-zero without carbon capture is possible but requires dramatic changes elsewhere such as much lower global energy demand — CCS functions as the substitute for demand reduction in mainstream climate pathways.
insights.speaker: Josh Gabbatiss
insights.so_what: The political economy favours CCS survival: it is the option that avoids asking economies to shrink energy demand, so support is resilient even when performance disappoints.
insights.quote: From an IPCC climate modelling perspective…reaching net-zero without CCS is far more expensive, disruptive and potentially out of reach.
insights.locator: What role is CCS expected to play in reaching net-zero? — 'When considering CCS for both emissions cuts and removals'

themes.theme: UK's £21.7bn cluster bet as the live policy test case

insights.claim: The UK has committed up to £21.7bn over 25 years to its first five carbon capture projects, with roughly three-quarters of that funding expected to come from levies on consumers rather than government budgets — a structure that insulates it from Treasury cuts but exposes it to energy-bill politics.
insights.speaker: Josh Gabbatiss
insights.so_what: The commonly cited raid-the-CCS-budget risk is overstated; the real political vulnerability is a cost-of-living backlash against levies on bills.
insights.quote: This is in spite of the fact that three quarters of the funding is expected to come from levies on consumers, rather than government budgets.
insights.locator: What are the UK's plans for scaling up CCS? — 'Some have suggested that this represents a large pot'

insights.claim: The UK's four named CCS clusters are the East Coast Cluster in north-east England and HyNet in north-west England and north Wales, both due in the late-2020s, followed by Acorn in north-east Scotland and Viking in the Humber around 2030, storing CO2 in offshore saline aquifers and depleted gas fields.
insights.speaker: Josh Gabbatiss
insights.so_what: These are the specific project names and dates to track for slippage — the late-2020s and 2030 milestones are the sector's nearest verifiable checkpoints.
insights.locator: What are the UK's plans for scaling up CCS? — 'The first two CCS clusters'

insights.claim: BP withdrew from one of the blue hydrogen facilities at the Teesside site at the end of 2025, with a data centre planned for the site instead — a direct substitution of AI-driven compute demand for a subsidised decarbonisation asset.
insights.speaker: Josh Gabbatiss
insights.so_what: Land, grid connections and industrial sites earmarked for hydrogen and CCS are now competing with data-centre economics — a repeatable pattern to watch across UK and EU industrial clusters.
insights.quote: (At the end of 2025, BP withdrew its involvement in one of the blue hydrogen facilities at the Teesside site. A data centre is planned for the site instead.)
insights.locator: What are the UK's plans for scaling up CCS? — 'They note that the gas-CCS power plants'

insights.claim: Carbon Tracker's analysis found the Net Zero Teesside gas-CCS plant run by BP and Equinor could cut emissions by around three-quarters versus an unabated gas plant, but only by a quarter if it relies on imported gas with high upstream emissions — making fuel sourcing, not capture technology, the dominant variable.
insights.speaker: Josh Gabbatiss
insights.so_what: Lifecycle emissions performance hinges on gas supply contracts; any gas-CCS asset's green credentials should be diligenced at the wellhead, not the stack.
insights.quote: The project could cut emissions by around three-quarters, relative to an unabated gas plant, says the report. But it adds that if the plant relies on imported gas with high upstream emissions, then it might only cut emissions by a quarter.
insights.locator: What are the UK's plans for scaling up CCS? — 'According to a report by Carbon Tracker'

insights.claim: Most upstream emissions from imported gas burned in UK gas-CCS plants would be released overseas and therefore not counted in the UK's official emissions inventory — an accounting boundary that lets a project look decarbonising domestically while shifting emissions abroad.
insights.speaker: Josh Gabbatiss
insights.so_what: Territorial carbon accounting creates arbitrage that flatters gas-CCS; a shift toward consumption-based or lifecycle accounting would reprice these assets sharply.
insights.quote: (Most of the upstream emissions from imported gas would be released overseas, meaning they would not be counted in the UK’s official emissions inventory.)
insights.locator: What are the UK's plans for scaling up CCS? — 'According to a report by Carbon Tracker'

insights.claim: The UK Climate Change Committee cut its recommended power and industry CCS capacity from 46MtCO2 to 41MtCO2 between its sixth and seventh carbon budget advice, with its CCS lead attributing the reduction partly to more opportunities to decarbonise other sectors than were visible five years earlier.
insights.speaker: Josh Gabbatiss
insights.so_what: A second official downgrade alongside the IEA's — the ratchet on CCS expectations is turning down consistently across independent advisory bodies.
insights.quote: partly because we see more opportunities for decarbonising the other sectors and reducing those residual emissions than we saw five years ago
insights.locator: What are the UK's plans for scaling up CCS? — 'Between the CCC's sixth and seventh carbon budget advice'

insights.claim: In the UK Climate Change Committee's latest net-zero pathway, carbon capture delivers only 2% of emissions cuts in 2030 and 8% in 2050 — rising to 15% if BECCS removals are counted — a modest contribution relative to the political and financial attention the technology receives.
insights.speaker: Josh Gabbatiss
insights.so_what: Even the most CCS-supportive official UK pathway has it delivering under a tenth of abatement — a useful sanity check against sector hype.
insights.quote: CCS contributes 2% of emissions cuts in 2030 and 8% in 2050
insights.locator: What are the UK's plans for scaling up CCS? — 'In the CCC's most recent net-zero pathway'

insights.claim: The UK Public Accounts Committee criticised the cluster-based approach in early 2025 for failing to direct CCUS support at the sectors that need it most, singling out cement, and attacked the high-risk use of public funds alongside slow technology progress.
insights.speaker: Josh Gabbatiss
insights.so_what: Parliamentary scrutiny is pushing toward re-sequencing subsidies away from geographic clusters and toward sector-targeted support — a plausible policy change to front-run.
insights.quote: does not ensure that financial support for CCUS is directed at the sectors which will need it most
insights.locator: What are the UK's plans for scaling up CCS? — 'A report by the Public Accounts Committee in early 2025'

insights.claim: Offshore Energies UK's head of energy policy Enrique Cornejo argues the UK must streamline cluster sequencing so cement emitters get a clear route to the CCS market, tying cost reduction explicitly to achieving economies of scale through continued deployment.
insights.speaker: Josh Gabbatiss
insights.so_what: Industry's ask is faster cluster sequencing — a concrete regulatory catalyst to watch that would unlock cement-sector capture orders.
insights.quote: It is indeed necessary to streamline the cluster sequencing process to ensure that emitters in sectors such as cement have a clear route to the CCS market.
insights.locator: What are the UK's plans for scaling up CCS? — 'Enrique Cornejo, head of energy policy'

insights.claim: Andrew Boswell, the energy analyst whose court challenge to Net Zero Teesside was unsuccessful, distinguishes between gas-CCS and non-gas applications, saying there may be a case for cement, lime and waste while maintaining that the case remains unproven.
insights.speaker: Josh Gabbatiss
insights.so_what: Litigation risk is concentrated on gas-CCS specifically; industrial and waste capture faces materially less legal opposition.
insights.quote: There may be a case for cement, lime and waste…However, the case is unproven
insights.locator: What are the UK's plans for scaling up CCS? — 'Dr Andrew Boswell, the energy analyst'
